transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
>> Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump is heading back to Washington, D.C.,
after a four-day trip in Asia.
NPR's Frank Ordonez reports Trump plans
to hold a press conference on the trip tomorrow
at the White House.
>> U.S. presidents typically hold a news conference
at the end of foreign trips in order to highlight all
that happened behind the scenes
and explain what was accomplished.
But President Trump left China without meeting with the press.
Now, China has a history of controlling the media,
including banning one U.S. reporter this trip
after she shouted a question during the event.
And it wasn't until the flight back
and after President Putin held his own press conference
that Trump announced on social media
that he would be holding a press conference at the White House.
In addition to discussing the historic trilateral meeting
with China and Russia,
Trump says he'll also be discussing trade deals
with Thailand and the Philippines.
Frank Ordonez, NPR News.
>> President Trump's financial disclosures today reveal
in September he bought and sold shares of NVIDIA.
Weeks before reports emerged
that the chipmaker's former CEO, Jensen Wong,
who's been a close Trump advisor, had an affair
with a woman suspected of spying for China.
Wong later resigned.
A recent string of tech outages has cut off access
to e-mail bank accounts and other everyday services,
and Piers Windsor-Johnson reports experts say a backup plan
can help when systems suddenly go down.
>> Most of the recent disruptions were outages
rather than data breaches.
Laurie Craner of Carnegie Mellon University
says the problems exposed how dependent people have become
on a small number of services.
>> For a bank account, you have another bank account
at another bank where, you know,
you can at least access cash or a credit card.
So that if you can't access money from one bank,
there's another place.
>> Craner recommends the same kind of backup for communication.
That can mean keeping a second e-mail account
with a different provider
and making sure text messages don't depend on the same system.
She says important files should also be saved
on a personal device instead of only in the cloud.
Windsor-Johnson, NPR News.
>> A new study from Boston University researchers
finds a possible way to test for the degenerative brain disease CTE.
Here's WBUR's Amy Secklow.
>> The researchers found that the players with high-stage CTE
had high amounts of a specific protein in their blood.
Senior study author Michael Olosco
cautioned that these are still early-stage findings
with a small sample size.
But he called the discovery a game changer.
>> If I'm a football player concerned,
it tells me that we're not far away
from being able to diagnose it during life
and then getting to the point where we can effectively start
treatment trials.
>> He says we could be within five years
of an FDA approval for the test
if the findings hold up to additional study.
For NPR News, I'm Amy Secklow.
>> It's NPR News.
A new survey finds more than four in 10 adults in the USA.
They've had at least one serious financial hardship
in the past year.
NPR's Jennifer Ledin reports
that is the highest level in a decade.
The most common hardships?
Having to borrow money from family or friends to pay bills
and not paying an important bill in full.
That's according to the American Family Survey
by researchers at Brigham Young University.
People also reported being hungry,
forgoing medical care,
having to move in with someone else,
or losing housing altogether.
The poll also finds broad concern
about being able to afford a home or family.
In fact, when younger adults were asked
what's the most important thing to do before having a child,
being financially stable topped the list.
Looking ahead, most Americans of all ages
say the biggest threat to their finances is inflation.
Jennifer Ledin, NPR News.
>> The Trump administration wants the U.S. Supreme Court
to allow it to cancel $16 billion
in Biden-era climate grants.
The Environmental Protection Agency
is asking the high court to review its cuts
to the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund,
also known as Green Bank.
The program involves public, quasi-public,
or non-profit financing entities
that leverage public and private capital
to pursue goals for clean energy projects
that reduce emissions.
If the U.S. Supreme Court takes up the case
and rules in the EPA's favor,
the grant cancellation case
would become the largest of its kind in U.S. history.
It's NPR News.

topics.text: President Trump returns to Washington after four-day Asia trip, plans White House press conference
Trump's financial disclosures show September NVIDIA share trades before CEO Jensen Huang's affair report
Recent tech outages prompt experts to recommend backup email, bank accounts, and saved files
Boston University study finds possible blood test for CTE in football players
Survey finds over 40% of U.S. adults faced serious financial hardship, highest in a decade
Trump administration asks Supreme Court to allow cancellation of $16 billion in Biden-era climate grants
